title: Tabitha Sable - Curses! A Story of UNIX Interface Hardware and Software Co-Evolution
speaker: Tabitha Sable
summary: A history of how the hardware used to interact with Unix (printing telegraphs, paper teletypes, video display terminals, then bitmapped workstations) co-evolved with the software written for it. Sable traces the line from teletype-era ioctl and stty complexity, through Berkeley's cheap ADM-3A glass terminals, ex/vi visual mode and termcap, to Ken Arnold extracting curses from vi, with Rogue as curses' killer application. She continues through terminfo, X Windows, pcurses/ncurses and the start of modern open source, arguing that old interface decisions stay sticky across generations of software. There is little game design content; its value is as genre-infrastructure history.

insights.claim: Curses was created when Ken Arnold lifted vi's screen-redraw code into a library that computes the minimum cursor movements needed to update a character-cell display, and Rogue became its canonical killer app.
insights.detail: It shipped with 4BSD around 1980. Sable notes Rogue was not the first curses program: Arnold told a panel at the first Roguelike Celebration that he first wrote tools for his own use, but Rogue was certainly the killer app.
insights.quote: Ken Arnold took the code, lifted it out of VI and wrapped it up in a nice library wrapper

insights.claim: Because the many glass terminals of the late 1970s were mutually incompatible, Berkeley's ex/vi introduced termcap, a database of terminal descriptions that let full-screen 'visual mode' work device-independently.
insights.detail: Visual mode, showing the file as you edited it instead of line-oriented teletype-style editing, was revolutionary. The termcap library parsing terminal descriptions was very important and popular; it later had performance problems, which Mary Ann Horton's 1982 'new curses and terminfo' addressed with compiled, human-readable descriptions.
insights.quote: The termcap library that can parse the descriptions of terminals and use them to know how to do the things that the visual mode needed

insights.claim: The hjkl movement keys used in vi and roguelikes come from the ADM-3A terminal, whose keyboard had no arrow keys but printed arrows on h, j, k and l.
insights.detail: The ADM-3A was famous as the first video display terminal under $1,000 and was installed in University of California labs as BSD began. Sable says these are the characters you use to move around to this day.
insights.quote: there are no arrow keys on the keyboard but h, j, k, and l have aroh -- arrows printed on them

insights.claim: The default 80-by-24 character size of terminal emulators today comes from the DEC VT100, the de facto standard terminal of the late 1970s.
insights.detail: The VT100 supported upper and lowercase, screen blanking and cursor movement; the VT220 later took over as smaller, cheaper and fancier.
insights.quote: This particular terminal is also the one that introduced today's standard of 80 by 24 characters

insights.claim: Unix's tty device names, the 'not a typewriter' error and the term baud rate are all leftovers from teletype hardware.
insights.detail: Device nodes were named /dev/tty plus the number of the teletype; ioctl was designed to configure teletype I/O and the first Unix manual noted a heavy predisposition toward Model 37 teletypes. Baud rate comes from the 5-bit code teletypes used.
insights.quote: the device nodes were named slash dev tty and a number because it was which number teletype it was

insights.claim: Pavel Curtis cloned Bell Labs' improved curses in a clean-room way so people outside Bell Labs could use it; that pcurses languished after 1986 and was picked up in 1993 as ncurses.
insights.detail: Sable places this within the licensing concerns that led to the free Unix clone projects, 4.3BSD-era removal of AT&T code, Linux in 1991, and Slackware and NetBSD in 1993.
insights.quote: clone the new curses library in a clean room way so that outside of Bell Labs folks could appreciate the improvement to curses

insights.claim: Interface conventions are sticky: the software people are used to shapes what they want next, so old hardware limits persist for decades.
insights.detail: Sable's closing argument: Visual Studio Code is more advanced than Vim yet you can still turn on vi key bindings, influenced by ADM-3As lacking arrow keys, and the Unix shell still talks to a teletype.
